title: response-layering-scribble
content:
Quick brain dump on 'response layering' as a lightweight pattern for balancing cost/fidelity/latency at the response composition level. Treating this as a personal sketchpad — lots of half-baked ideas, experiments, and open questions.

Context / motivation:
- Problem: product teams want deterministic UX but also tight control over cost and latency. Current options: single-model with quality tradeoffs, or coarse routing to cheaper models that sometimes fail.
- Idea: compose answers from a small set of incremental 'layers' (micro-responses) that are merged into a final response. Each layer is a targeted, cheaper call (or cached fragment) that can be evaluated, validated, and selectively included.

What a "layer" is (sketch):
- Layer 0: metadata + secure checks (auth, content policy, deterministic scaffolding). Very cheap, fast.
- Layer 1: retrieve/cached facts (embeddings/KB lookups, deterministic templates) — small tokens, ideally cached.
- Layer 2: cheap LLM pass — short answer, low-context, low-cost model for coverage.
- Layer 3: selective fidelity pass — only triggered for sections flagged as uncertain or high-value; higher-cost model or more tokens.
- Layer 4: formatting/postprocess (structured output, tools).

Key behaviors (implementation notes):
- Layers are independent calls that can run in parallel or sequentially depending on dependencies (e.g., L3 may need L2 output).
- Each layer emits: token_count, confidence_score, provenance (model id, prompt hash), latency. These feed the merge policy.
- Merge policy: deterministic rules + ML gating. E.g., if L2.confidence > 0.8 and cost threshold hit, skip L3. If L2 uncertain and user has premium tier, run L3 by default.
- Inline fallbacks: for regions of the response (paragraphs, bullets) we can pick per-region layers rather than whole-response.

Concrete user stories (prioritized):
1) As a consumer-facing assistant, I want short immediate answers (~1-2 sentences) returned in <200ms while a more thoughtful expansion streams later, so product feels snappy.
2) As a platform engineer, I want per-request cost breakdown by layer so I can build budget-aware routing and quotas.
3) As a feature owner, I want to mark parts of the prompt as 'safety-sensitive' so those sections always get high-fidelity review.
4) As an admin, I want automatic degradation to cached layers when Dedicated capacity is exhausted.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Basic runtime: orchestrate 2 layers (cache/retrieval + cheap LLM) with merge policy based on confidence heuristics.
- Telemetry: per-layer token/latency/cost logged and surfaced in Console for a sample workspace.
- Policy knobs: enable/disable layer 3 per-route; per-customer credit threshold to gate higher layers.
- Feature toggle: streaming the cheap layer first, then patch higher-fidelity fragments via delta stream.

Experiment ideas / hypothesis tests:
- A/B: baseline single-model vs 2-layer (cheap + selective high-fidelity) for average token cost and user satisfaction measured by click-through/explicit rating. Hypothesis: ~25% token savings with <5% dip in satisfaction.
- Micro-benchmark: per-section selective L3 only for lines with has_questions(L2) or contains_named_entities(L2).
- Caching: measure hit-rate for Layer 1 (KB) across common prompts; find TTL sweet spot.

Telemetry & metrics to capture:
- cost_per_request_by_layer, avg_latency_first_byte, avg_latency_final_merge, #layers_triggered_per_request, merge_rewrites_rate, user_satisfaction_signal (NPS/rating), fallback_rate_to_cache, high-fidelity_trigger_rate_by-customer-tier.

Operational concerns / risks:
- Complexity: More orchestration means more failure modes (partially applied deltas, inconsistency). Need idempotent merge operations and clear rollback.
- Privacy/compliance: multiple model calls might touch different token retention policies. Must tag layers with retention and ensure private customers never send certain layers to hosted models.
- Debuggability: need clear traces showing which layer contributed each token. Console UX change required.

Integration touches (quick map):
- Serving runtime: parallel request fan-out, KV cache hooks, per-call kernel selection.
- Console: new per-layer timeline view, cost breakdown, merge diffs.
- Routing: per-tenant gating for high-fidelity layers and Dedicated fallback rules.
- SDK: new param 'response_layers' (array of layer specs) and streaming semantics for partial merges.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to design a concise prompt language to express layering intent without exploding prompt size? (prompt macros?)
- Merge conflict resolution: prefer higher-fidelity content by default, but for deterministic UX maybe prefer first-byte (low-latency) unless replacement confidence delta > X.
- API ergonomics: stream cheap layer as 'provisional' with explicit replace events for updated sections vs patch-based insertion. Which is easier for client apps?
- Cost accounting model: bill by actual tokens plus a small orchestration surcharge? or amortize across layers?

Short-term next steps (my plan):
- Spike: implement a prototype in the local runtime that runs L2 (gpt-lite) + optional L3 (gpt-mid) and produces a merged JSON that annotates provenance (2 days).
- Telemetry hook: log per-layer cost/latency to our internal dev console (1 week).
- UX pattern: sketch two client UXs for streaming provisional + patches vs patch-only (1 day).
- Kick a sync with Maya (retrieval) and Ethan (console) to align data model — pinged them, they said "ok this week".

Random parking-lot ideas (not required for MVP):
- Layer compaction: run periodic background process to combine layers into a single cached final for common queries.
- User-configurable fidelity lanes: allow end-users to slide a control (economy -> accurate) and set per-session layer budgets.
- Token-level provenance: enable 'hover' in UI to show which layer generated a snippet.

Notes to self: keep the initial scope tiny (2 layers + streaming provisional). The hardest part will be merge semantics and UX expectations around stochastic replacements. If we can make the early cheap pass very high-precision for surface-level answers (facts & short summaries), we get most of the perceived snappiness win.

End of scribble. Will iteratively formalize into a short PRD if spike looks promising.

-- Tomasz
